messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: 25% of time spent in check_range?
parts:
Hey,

So I'm playing with a simple model in Stan and it was running a bit slower than I would have expected.  After a profiling run, it turned out that around 25% of the time was being spent in check_range().  I would have expected that these checks would have been disabled with -DNDEBUG at compile time (which turns off these checks in Eigen), but apparently not.  An easy fix is to wrap the body of check_range with an #ifndef NDEBUG block.

Anyone have any thoughts?  For reference, this was with clang++ and -O3 on Linux.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] 25% of time spent in check_range?
parts:
On 8/17/12 4:39 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> Hey,
>
> So I'm playing with a simple model in Stan and it was running a bit slower than I would have expected. After a
> profiling run, it turned out that around 25% of the time was being spent in check_range(). I would have expected that
> these checks would have been disabled with -DNDEBUG at compile time (which turns off these checks in Eigen), but
> apparently not. An easy fix is to wrap the body of check_range with an #ifndef NDEBUG block.
>
> Anyone have any thoughts? For reference, this was with clang++ and -O3 on Linux.

My first thought is "yikes".

My second thought is that we've found g++ to
be a bit faster.

My third thought is that putting in flags is a good
idea that we should finally get around to doing!

I think we should follow Eigen, which turns off range
checking if either the flag NDEBUG or flag EIGEN_NO_DEBUG
is used (i.e., called with -DNDEBUG or -DEIGEN_NO_DEBUG).

So I'd suggest STAN_NO_DEBUG and calling the error checking
under the condition that !(STAN_NO_DEBUG || NDEBUG).

We'd then want to be able to pass options through calls
to stanc. That in turn means we can't precompile object
files for the relevant calls, at least if we turn things
off at a fairly low level.

I'm curious as to why it's so expensive. The function
is inline, passes three size_t values and a const char*,
with a body that's a simple if statement that's
always false. I wonder if it's somehow
opportunistically pre-allocating for the stringstream?
Or the size is causing it not to be inlined.
Just in case, I broke out a raise_range_error.

So it now looks like this:

void raise_range_error(size_t max,
size_t i,
const char* msg,
size_t idx) {
std::stringstream s;
s << "INDEX OPERATOR [] OUT OF BOUNDS"
<< "; index=" << i
<< "; lower bound=1"
<< "; upper bound=" << max
<< "; index position=" << idx
<< "; " << msg
<< std::endl;
throw std::out_of_range(s.str());
}

inline
void check_range(size_t max,
size_t i,
const char* msg,
size_t idx) {
if (i < 1 || i > max)
raise_range_error(max,i,msg,idx);
}

I pushed the change.

Should the test for NDEBUG or STAN_NO_DEBUG be on the
body of check range as Marcus suggests? That would be my
inclination because it should be sufficient
to make sure check_range is inlined away. We just have
to be sure not to precompile check_range if we do it
this way!

We can also turn off checks in the probability
functions the same way. Some of those will be expensive
if we test that matrices are positive definite, etc.

- Bob

On Fri, Aug 17, 2012 at 5:12 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
On 8/17/12 4:39 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
Hey,

So I'm playing with a simple model in Stan and it was running a bit slower than I would have expected.  After a
profiling run, it turned out that around 25% of the time was being spent in check_range().  I would have expected that
these checks would have been disabled with -DNDEBUG at compile time (which turns off these checks in Eigen), but
apparently not.  An easy fix is to wrap the body of check_range with an #ifndef NDEBUG block.

Anyone have any thoughts?  For reference, this was with clang++ and -O3 on Linux.

My first thought is "yikes".
Mine too!

My second thought is that we've found g++ to
be a bit faster.
I haven't tested with g++, as I lack the patience for it's compile time while working.

My third thought is that putting in flags is a good
idea that we should finally get around to doing!

I think we should follow Eigen, which turns off range
checking if either the flag NDEBUG or flag EIGEN_NO_DEBUG
is used (i.e., called with -DNDEBUG or -DEIGEN_NO_DEBUG).

So I'd suggest STAN_NO_DEBUG and calling the error checking
under the condition that !(STAN_NO_DEBUG || NDEBUG).

My reading of the Eigen docs suggests that they use EIGEN_NO_DEBUG on it's own and turn that on or off based on the status of NDEBUG.  Seems like a reasonable pattern as it allows turning debugging off or on in each library separately and simplifies the test conditions.

I.E., we have something like

#ifdef NDEBUG
#  ifndef STAN_NO_DEBUG
#    define STAN_NO_DEBUG
#  endif
#endif

in a global header file and then in stan the blocks are just

#ifdef STAN_NO_DEBUG
...
#endif

We'd then want to be able to pass options through calls
to stanc.  That in turn means we can't precompile object
files for the relevant calls, at least if we turn things
off at a fairly low level.

I'm curious as to why it's so expensive.  The function
is inline, passes three size_t values and a const char*,
with a body that's a simple if statement that's
always false.  I wonder if it's somehow
opportunistically pre-allocating for the stringstream?
Or the size is causing it not to be inlined.
Just in case, I broke out a raise_range_error.

So it now looks like this:

    void raise_range_error(size_t max,
                             size_t i,
                             const char* msg,
                             size_t idx) {
          std::stringstream s;
          s << "INDEX OPERATOR [] OUT OF BOUNDS"
            << "; index=" << i
            << "; lower bound=1"
            << "; upper bound=" << max
            << "; index position=" << idx
            << "; " << msg
            << std::endl;
          throw std::out_of_range(s.str());
      }

      inline
      void check_range(size_t max,
                       size_t i,
                       const char* msg,
                       size_t idx) {
        if (i < 1 || i > max)
          raise_range_error(max,i,msg,idx);
      }

I pushed the change.
I can test to see if this performs better.  In which case it was probably just clang++ ignoring the inline directive.  It may also be the case that a branch hint would help things.

Should the test for NDEBUG or STAN_NO_DEBUG be on the
body of check range as Marcus suggests?  That would be my
inclination because it should be sufficient
to make sure check_range is inlined away.  We just have
to be sure not to precompile check_range if we do it
this way!
I'd say in the body, as check_range is to be inlined anyway.  It may miss some cases (like if someone precompiles libstan.a without NDEBUG) but that seems like small fry.

We can also turn off checks in the probability
functions the same way.  Some of those will be expensive
if we test that matrices are positive definite, etc.

Those tests are more necessary in sampling though, as if they're violated the sampler needs to know about it.  I would hesitate to turn them off unless we're certain they're not necessary.

Cheers,
Marcus

> On Aug 17, 2012, at 11:29 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
>> I haven't tested with g++, as I lack the patience for it's compile time while working.

On 8/17/12 5:36 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Compile time is annoying but, in my experience, almost any model I fit, I end up fitting over and over again (which we
> can now do in Stan without recompiling). So I think run time is much more important than compile time, even for simple
> models.

Wait until you have g++ configured to use -O3 (see
Jiqiang's latest directions for RStan on how to do
this).

The run times are much faster, but compile time slows
to a crawl.

So it's a tradeoff depending on what you want to do.

If you have a big model and know it works, -O3 on g++ is
the way to go. Otherwise, I've just been using -O0.

For something like 8 Schools, which is trivial, you won't
notice the slowdown in runtime, but you will notice the
speedup in compile time going from -O2 to -O0.

At least one plus is that most of our syntax errors
are found in the stanc model translation phase. Everything
stanc translates should at least compile in C++.

- Bob

>
> Agreed for the standard use case.

How much time you spend at a given setting is easy
to write down:

compile + N * run

where N is the number of times you run.

The issue is you don't know how big N is until you see how
it works.

With eight schools, compile time at -O2 is 5s and run time
is 0.01s or something like that. You need to run a whole
lot of times to make up for that compile time. -O0 might
compile in 2s and run in .1s.

> That said, I'm doing things which should ideally be unusual for most users. For
> instance, I'm tweaking the model repeatedly to find performance issues and better ways to write the model. This
> tweaking and profiling is typically done on small subsets of data or toy examples before scaling up to the full dataset
> so the sampling runtime is relatively. At that point the compile time tends to take precedence...

How does that work? The performance bottlenecks
change dramatically when you move to more optimization.

- Bob

> That said, I'm doing things which should ideally be unusual for most users.  For
instance, I'm tweaking the model repeatedly to find performance issues and better ways to write the model.  This
tweaking and profiling is typically done on small subsets of data or toy examples before scaling up to the full dataset
so the sampling runtime is relatively.  At that point the compile time tends to take precedence...

How does that work?  The performance bottlenecks
change dramatically when you move to more optimization.

I always compile with -O3, but use clang++ instead of g++.  The bottlenecks change a little bit, but not much.  Most optimization of Stan models is more about reducing the number of variables that get instantiated than about compiler level optimization.

For instance, I had a line that was:

x <- x + a*exp(-lambda*dt);

where dt is a constant.

Changing it to

x <- x + a*exp(lambda*ndt);

where ndt was precomputed to be the negative, reduced the overall cost by ~30% or so.

Cheers,
Marcus
